She suddenly felt a strong desire to go to the front door and see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of having any other motive? Captain Wentworth must already be out of sight. She rose from her chair, determined to go. One half of her mind should not always presume to be wiser than the other, or accuse it of being worse than it was. She would check the rain. But a moment later she was driven back by Captain Wentworth’s entrance. He came with a group of ladies and gentlemen who were evidently friends of his, and whom he must have joined just below Milsom Street. The sight of her unsettled and confused him more visibly than she had ever seen before; he actually flushed. For the first time since they had met again, she felt that she was showing less emotion than he was. The last few moments had given her the advantage of preparation. The overwhelming, blinding confusion of the first surprise had already passed for her. Even so, she had plenty left to feel: agitation, pain, pleasure, something suspended between joy and misery.

He spoke to her, then turned away. His manner conveyed embarrassment. She could not have described it as cold or friendly with anything like the certainty with which she could call it embarrassed.

After a brief interval, however, he approached and spoke again. They exchanged questions about ordinary matters, neither probably learning much from the answers, while Anne remained acutely aware that he was less at ease than before. Spending so much time together had enabled them to speak with a fair appearance of calm indifference, but he could no longer manage it. Time had changed him, or Louisa had. He was self-conscious about something. He looked very well, with no sign that his health or spirits had suffered. He mentioned Uppercross and the Musgroves—even Louisa, whose name brought a fleeting return of his familiar, mischievously meaningful expression. Yet this was still Captain Wentworth uncomfortable, ill at ease, and unable to pretend otherwise.

Anne was not surprised, but was hurt, to see Elizabeth refusing to acknowledge him. She saw that he had noticed Elizabeth and that Elizabeth had noticed him; each had plainly recognized the other. Anne was certain he was ready, even expecting, to be greeted as an acquaintance. Instead she had the pain of watching her sister turn away with unwavering coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, which Miss Elliot had been awaiting with growing impatience, now pulled up, and the servant came inside to announce it.

“Jupiter,” he said when we reached the base of the tree, “come here. Was the skull nailed to the branch facing outward, or facing the wood?”

“Facing out, master, so the crows could reach the eyes easily, without any trouble.”

“Then which eye did you drop the beetle through—this one or that one?” Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes in turn.

“This one, master—the left eye, just like you told me.” But the eye the Black man pointed to was his right.

“That’s enough. We must try again.”

My friend, whose madness now seemed to me—or perhaps only appeared to seem—to contain some method, moved the peg marking where the beetle had fallen about three inches west of its original position. As before, he stretched the measuring tape from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, then extended it in a straight line for fifty feet. This indicated a spot several yards away from our previous digging.

We marked a circle around the new position, somewhat larger than the first, and took up our spades again. I was terribly tired, but although I hardly understood what had changed my mind, I no longer greatly resented the work demanded of me. Quite inexplicably, I had become interested—even excited. Perhaps something in Legrand’s extravagant behavior, some suggestion of forethought or careful calculation, had impressed me. I dug eagerly and occasionally caught myself looking with something very close to expectation for the imaginary treasure whose vision had driven my unfortunate companion mad. These strange thoughts were occupying me most strongly when, after perhaps an hour and a half of work, the dog’s furious howling interrupted us again. His earlier restlessness had evidently been nothing more than playfulness or a passing whim; now his cries had a fierce, serious note. When Jupiter tried once more to muzzle him, he resisted violently, then jumped into the hole and clawed frantically at the soil. Within seconds he had exposed a heap of human bones making up two complete skeletons, mixed with several metal buttons and what looked like the crumbling remains of woolen cloth. One or two thrusts of a spade brought up the blade of a large Spanish knife. As we dug deeper, three or four loose gold and silver coins appeared.

“One last word, Rose! Dearest Rose, only one!” Harry cried, flinging himself before her. “Had I been less—less fortunate, as the world would put it—had I been destined for a quiet, unnoticed life—had I been poor, ill, and powerless—would you have rejected me then? Or does this objection spring from my prospect of rising to wealth and distinction?”

“Do not compel me to answer,” Rose replied. “That question has no place here, and never will. To insist on it is unfair, almost cruel.”

“If your reply is what I scarcely dare hope,” Harry answered, “it will cast a little happiness on my solitary road and brighten the way ahead. It is no small matter to do so much with a handful of words for someone who loves you more than anything. Oh, Rose, for the sake of my passionate, lasting devotion, for everything I have endured for you and everything you condemn me to endure, answer this one question!”

“Then, had your circumstances been otherwise,” said Rose, “had your place been only a little above mine, instead of so very far; had I been able to offer you comfort and assistance in some modest, peaceful retreat, rather than be a stain and an obstacle among the ambitious and distinguished, I would have escaped this ordeal. I have every cause for happiness now, for great happiness; but then, Harry, I confess I would have been happier still.”

As Rose made this admission, memories of hopes she had cherished long ago as a girl crowded through her thoughts. They brought tears, as old hopes do when they return faded and withered, and those tears eased her heart.

“I cannot prevent this weakness, and it only strengthens my resolve,” Rose said, offering her hand. “I really must leave you now.”

“Promise me one thing,” said Harry. “Allow me once, and only once more—within a year, let us say, though it may be much sooner—to speak of this again, for the final time.”

“Not to urge me to abandon a decision I know is right,” Rose replied with a sorrowful smile. “That would achieve nothing.”

“No,” Harry said, “only to hear you repeat it, if you choose—repeat it finally. Whatever position or fortune I possess, I will place at your feet; and if you remain determined, I will make no effort, in anything I say or do, to alter your decision.”

“Then we shall agree to that,” Rose answered. “It is only one further sorrow, and perhaps by then I shall be better able to endure it.”

Once more she held out her hand.
